title: Making Deep Learning go Brrrr From First Principles
summary: If you want to keep your GPUs going brrrr, let's discuss the three components your system might be spending time on - compute, memory bandwidth, and overhead. One perspective on optimizing deep learning systems is that we'd like to maximize the time in the compute-bound regime.

title: GPU Performance Background User's Guide
summary: This guide provides background on the structure of a GPU, how operations are executed, and common limitations with deep learning operations. GPUs accelerate machine learning operations by performing calculations in parallel.

title: Get Started With Deep Learning Performance
summary: This is the landing page for our deep learning performance documentation. This page provides recommendations that apply to most deep learning operations. Even better performance can be achieved by tweaking operation parameters to efficiently use GPU resources.

title: Performance Tuning Guide (PyTorch)
summary: Performance Tuning Guide is a set of optimizations and best practices which can accelerate training and inference of deep learning models in PyTorch. Presented techniques often can be implemented by changing only a few lines of code.

title: PyTorch Profiler
summary: This recipe explains how to use PyTorch profiler and measure the time and memory consumption of the model's operators.

title: All About Rooflines (How To Scale Your Model, Part 1)
summary: When we run algorithms on hardware, we're bounded by three things: how fast our computer can do math (OPs/second), the bandwidth available for moving data around (bytes/second), and the total memory available to store data (bytes). These roofline constraints let us bound the time of a computation.

title: How To Scale Your Model
summary: Training LLMs often feels like alchemy, but understanding and optimizing the performance of your models doesn't have to. This book aims to demystify the science of scaling language models: how TPUs (and GPUs) work and how they communicate with each other.

title: Tuning Spark
summary: Because of the in-memory nature of most Spark computations, Spark programs can be bottlenecked by any resource in the cluster: CPU, network bandwidth, or memory. Serialization plays an important role in the performance of any distributed application.

title: Dask Best Practices
summary: It is easy to get started with Dask's APIs, but using them well requires some experience. This page contains suggestions for Dask best practices and includes solutions to common Dask problems.

title: Introduction to torch.compile
summary: torch.compile makes PyTorch code run faster by JIT-compiling PyTorch code into optimized kernels, while requiring minimal code changes.

title: NVIDIA Nsight Systems User Guide
summary: Nsight Systems does not require any application changes to enable profiling. You typically only want to profile the region(s) of your application containing some or all of the performance-critical code.

title: A guide to LLM inference and performance
summary: We need to know if our inference is compute bound or memory bound so that we can make optimizations in the right area. Calculating the operations per byte possible on a given GPU and comparing it to the arithmetic intensity of our model's attention layers reveals where the bottleneck is.

title: What Is Isaac Sim? (Isaac Sim Documentation)
summary: Import robots and scenes from URDF, MJCF, Onshape CAD, or USD. Simulate with PhysX or Newton, add RTX and physics-based sensors, generate synthetic data, prepare robots for Isaac Lab, and validate robot stacks with ROS 2.

title: Getting Started With Isaac Sim (NVIDIA learning modules)
summary: This collection of modules will guide you through building, simulating, and working with robots in NVIDIA Isaac Sim: robot construction and control using OmniGraph and ROS 2, URDF import and physics configuration, synthetic data generation with Replicator, and Software-in-the-Loop testing.

title: Isaac Sim Basic Usage Tutorial
summary: This tutorial covers the basics of Isaac Sim, including navigating the GUI, adding objects to the stage, looking up basic properties of objects, and running simulations. You will go from a blank stage to a moving robot.

title: Isaac Sim Quick Install
summary: The Quick Install can be used for demos and to get a quick working idea of what the full product can do. After completing the quick install, you can create a room with a robot in it.

title: Isaac Sim Core API Tutorial Series
summary: The Core API tutorials are for beginner NVIDIA Isaac Sim users. This tutorial series explains how to create scripted scenes, control wheeled robots and manipulators, coordinate tasks, and add physics-ready props.

title: Perception Data Generation (Replicator) in Isaac Sim
summary: Isaac Sim Replicator offers various tools and workflows for synthetic data generation (SDG), primarily using the omni.replicator extension. The examples and tutorials showcase domain randomization, sensor simulation, and data collection.

title: ROS 2 tutorials (Isaac Sim)
summary: Isaac Sim is connected to ROS through the ROS 2 bridge extension. We recommend ROS 2 Humble and Jazzy with NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

title: Robot Setup (Isaac Sim)
summary: These tools and tutorials detail the different importers and exporters for converting assets to and from the USD (Universal Scene Description) format and how you can build custom robots in the simulator.

title: Welcome to Isaac Lab
summary: Isaac Lab is a unified and modular framework for robot learning that aims to simplify common workflows in robotics research (such as reinforcement learning, learning from demonstrations, and motion planning). It supports NVIDIA Isaac Sim for photo-realistic scenes and RTX rendering.

title: isaac-sim/IsaacSim
summary: NVIDIA Isaac Sim is a simulation platform built on NVIDIA Omniverse, designed to develop, test, train, and deploy AI-powered robots in realistic virtual environments. It supports importing robotic systems from common formats such as URDF, MJCF, and CAD.

title: Isaac Sim - Robotics Simulation and Synthetic Data Generation
summary: NVIDIA Isaac Sim is an open source reference framework built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for robotics simulation, testing, and synthetic data generation in physically based virtual environments.

title: THUDM/slime
summary: slime is an LLM training framework for RL scaling, providing two core capabilities: High-Performance Training, connecting Megatron with SGLang; and Flexible Data Generation through custom data generation interfaces and server-based engines.

title: slime documentation
summary: slime is an LLM post-training framework for RL scaling. Explore LLM reinforcement learning with slime: understand the rollout-reward-train loop, compare system choices, and export a starting experiment recipe.

title: slime Environment setup
summary: This page prepares the environment used by every generated recipe; the tutorial explains the full RL workflow. Use the provided Docker images to get a compatible SGLang, Megatron, and patch stack.

title: slime Usage Guide
summary: When using slime, parameters are primarily passed for the following purposes: to allocate a portion of the GPUs in the cluster for training and another portion for inference; to load Megatron for the training portion; to load SGLang for the inference portion.

title: Tutorial: build and understand an RL experiment (slime)
summary: Choose a model, watch the GPU layout change, try alternatives, and download the resulting shell. The loop: prompts, SGLang samples responses, reward or verifier, Megatron policy update, updated weights back to SGLang, checkpoint and held-out evaluation.

title: Understand the RL system you are building (slime)
summary: Placement owns GPUs, scheduling orders work, precision changes arithmetic, and serving topology divides inference work. A synchronous round generates responses, computes rewards, trains, and distributes new weights; with colocation rollout and training share GPUs.

title: slime Customization Guide
summary: slime provides extensive customization capabilities through function path arguments. These allow you to inject custom logic at various stages of the training and rollout pipeline without modifying the core codebase.

title: Debugging (slime)
summary: During the development of slime, it is often necessary to check if the model's precision is correct. Check if the generated rollout is coherent and whether Megatron successfully loaded the checkpoint.

title: Profiling (slime)
summary: In slime, we can perform detailed performance analysis of the rollout process using the profiling interface provided by SGLang.

title: Agentic RL Training Roadmap (slime)
summary: slime is not limited to single-turn RL. Its main advantage for agentic training is the combination of high-performance training, SGLang rollout serving, and pluggable data-generation interfaces, suitable for multi-turn tool use and sandbox environments.

title: Fault Tolerance (slime)
summary: slime checks SGLang engines, removes failed engines from service, and restarts them before the next weight update. This recovery workflow requires the Ray cluster to remain running.

title: slime: An SGLang-Native Post-Training Framework for RL Scaling
summary: We present slime, a post-training framework designed to be versatile, with a fully customizable rollout interface and flexible training setups (colocated or decoupled, synchronous or asynchronous, RL or SFT cold start), and performant, integrating SGLang for inference and Megatron-LM for training.

title: CS231A Course Notes 3: Epipolar Geometry
summary: In general, it is not possible to recover the entire structure of the 3D world from just one image, due to the intrinsic ambiguity of the 3D to the 2D mapping. The notes cover the Essential Matrix, the Fundamental Matrix and the Eight-Point Algorithm.

title: CS231A Course Notes 4: Stereo Systems and Structure from Motion
summary: In these lecture notes, we will discuss how to recover information about the 3D scene from multiple 2D images. One of the most fundamental problems in multiple view geometry is triangulation.

title: Computer Vision II: Multiple View Geometry (TUM)
summary: The lecture introduces the basic concepts of image formation - perspective projection and camera motion. The goal is to reconstruct the three-dimensional world and the camera motion from multiple images, using correspondences and constraints that allow to compute motion and 3D structure.

title: Multiple View Geometry Ch.5: Reconstruction from Two Views: Linear Algorithms
summary: Chapter 5 of the Multiple View Geometry lecture (Prof. Daniel Cremers): the reconstruction problem, the epipolar constraint, the eight-point algorithm, structure reconstruction, the four-point algorithm and the uncalibrated case.

title: Multiple View Geometry Ch.6: Reconstruction from Multiple Views
summary: Chapter 6 of the Multiple View Geometry lecture: from two views to multiple views, preimage and coimage from multiple views, rank constraints, the multiple-view matrix, relation to epipolar constraints and multiple-view reconstruction algorithms.

title: Two-view geometry (CMU 16-385 Lecture 12)
summary: Two-view geometry lecture of CMU 16-385 Computer Vision. Overview of today's lecture: triangulation, epipolar geometry, essential matrix, fundamental matrix, 8-point algorithm.

title: Geometry-based Methods in Vision (CMU 16-822)
summary: The course focuses on the geometric aspects of computer vision: the geometry of image formation and its use for 3D reconstruction and calibration. The objective of the course is to introduce the formal tools and results that are necessary for developing multi-view reconstruction algorithms.

title: COLMAP Tutorial: image-based 3D reconstruction
summary: This tutorial covers image-based 3D reconstruction by demonstrating the processing steps in COLMAP. Image-based 3D reconstruction traditionally first recovers a sparse representation of the scene and the camera poses using Structure-from-Motion, then Multi-View Stereo recovers a dense one.

title: kornia.geometry.epipolar
summary: Functions for two-view epipolar geometry, as used in Structure from Motion (SfM) and two-view pose estimation: estimate fundamental and essential matrices, recover the relative pose, score correspondences and triangulate.

title: Lecture 14 - Multi-View Geometry and Structure from Motion (Middlebury CS1053)
summary: Epipolar geometry: essential and fundamental matrices; finding the fundamental matrix from 2D correspondences; 8-point algorithm; find R, t from E. Multi-view geometry: reprojection error, pose estimation and triangulation problems; structure from motion demo using COLMAP.

title: Multiview 3D Geometry in Computer Vision (UMN CSci 5980)
summary: Multiview geometry is a core branch in computer vision that studies the 3D spatial relationship between cameras and scenes. The course covers multiview geometry including perspective projection, epipolar geometry, point triangulation, camera resectioning, and bundle adjustment.

title: Absolute camera orientation given set of relative camera pairs (PyTorch3D bundle adjustment)
summary: Given an optical system of N cameras with extrinsics in SE(3) and a set of relative camera positions that map between coordinate frames of randomly selected pairs of cameras, we search for the absolute extrinsic parameters consistent with the relative camera motions.

title: CS231A Course Notes 1: Camera Models
summary: The camera is one of the most essential tools in computer vision. How do we model a camera? These notes start from the pinhole camera model and cover projection of a 3D scene onto the image plane.

title: CS231A: Computer Vision, From 3D Perception to 3D Reconstruction and beyond
summary: An introduction to concepts and applications in computer vision primarily dealing with geometry and 3D understanding. Topics include: cameras and projection models, shape reconstruction from stereo, depth estimation and optical/scene flow, 6D pose estimation and object tracking.

title: Multiple View Geometry Ch.2: Representing a Moving Scene
summary: Chapter 2 of the Multiple View Geometry lecture (Prof. Daniel Cremers): the origins of 3D reconstruction, 3D space and rigid body motion, the Lie group SO(3), the Lie group SE(3), representing the camera motion, Euler angles.

title: 16-385 Computer Vision (CMU)
summary: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to computer vision. Major topics include image processing, detection and recognition, geometry-based and physics-based vision and video analysis, including 2D transformations, camera models, two-view geometry, stereo and structure from motion.

title: An Invitation to 3D Vision: A Tutorial for Everyone
summary: An Invitation to 3D Vision: A Tutorial for Everyone. The title came from a legendary book by Yi Ma, Stefano Soatto, Jana Kosecka, and Shankar S. Sastry; the tutorial is meant to be the first gentle invitation card for beginners to 3D vision and its applications.

title: A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics
topic: Lie groups for 3D rotation and pose
summary: A Lie group is an old mathematical abstract object. In robotics it is used in estimation, particularly motion estimation for navigation. In this paper, we will walk through the most basic principles of the Lie theory, with the aim of conveying clear and useful ideas for robot estimation.

title: kornia.geometry
summary: The kornia.geometry module provides essential geometric transformations for computer vision tasks, including 2D and 3D image manipulation. It includes submodules for image transforms, camera models, coordinate conversions, linear algebra operations, and depth map processing.

title: kornia.geometry.conversions
summary: Functions for converting between various geometric representations, such as angles, Euclidean and homogeneous coordinates, homographies, quaternions, rotation matrices, and Euler angles.

title: kornia.geometry.camera
summary: Camera models that map 3D points to pixels and back. The module provides functions for projecting 3D points to a 2D image plane, with perspective and orthographic projections, as well as distortion models.

title: Transformation (Open3D)
summary: The geometry types of Open3D have a number of transformation methods. This tutorial shows how to use translate, rotate, scale, and transform on 3D geometry such as meshes and point clouds.

title: Point cloud (Open3D)
summary: This tutorial demonstrates basic usage of a point cloud. Voxel downsampling uses a regular voxel grid to create a uniformly downsampled point cloud from an input point cloud. The PointCloud geometry type has bounding volumes that can also be used to crop the geometry.

title: ICP registration (Open3D)
summary: This tutorial demonstrates the ICP (Iterative Closest Point) registration algorithm, a mainstay of geometric registration. The input are two point clouds and an initial transformation that roughly aligns the source point cloud to the target point cloud; the output is a refined transformation.

title: Camera position optimization using differentiable rendering (PyTorch3D)
summary: We will first initialize a renderer with a starting position for the camera, use it to generate an image, compute a loss with the reference image, and finally backpropagate through the entire pipeline to update the position of the camera.
